<reason>CON (Side A) built the stronger route: a consistent empirical pattern (Mexico, Britain, Chile, Denmark, menu labels) showing deployed environmental policies shifted purchases but not weight, contrasted with behavioral programs that moved weight within a comparable ~3-year window. PRO's response—that every real-world case was "in miniature"—was pressed by CON's Q1 into an explicit concession that no jurisdiction shows environmental policy reducing obesity, and PRO's reciprocal demand was answered by CON's point that its programs at least moved bodies in those reached. CON also caught PRO's inconsistency on calorie labeling (listed as an environmental tool, then disowned as "information"), which PRO never resolved. PRO's best live argument—the reach/equity asymmetry ("environment needs no cooperation")—was genuinely strong and honestly argued, and reformulation was a plausible mechanism reaching the pantry. But CON blunted it twice: schools as a compulsory, income-blind population default (PRO's closing wrongly lumped this under "enrollment"), and Britain's reformulation coexisting with rising childhood obesity. CON's closing directly flipped PRO's key phrase ("universal coverage of a null effect is not reach"), while PRO's closing did not engage the schools point or the Britain outcome. Two clipped turns and a slightly stretched Quebec claim are minor costs for A; PRO's honest A1 concession and clean framing keep it competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was CON's Q1 forcing PRO's admission in B4.1 that no jurisdiction has reduced obesity via the environmental approach, followed by CON's closing reversal of PRO's "in the people they reach" line: environmental policy reaches everyone but has moved no one's weight, while schools already put every child—including the 9pm gas-station parent's—in the room. PRO's closing never answered the schools-as-universal-default point.</best_rebuttal>
